headline: Maine awards $299,057 for coastal habitat planning in four communities
dek: The one-time grants will fund marsh, road-crossing and natural-resource planning in Boothbay, Gouldsboro, Addison and the Popham area.
body: Maine's Office of Community Affairs has awarded $299,057 for four coastal habitat-planning projects that officials say are intended to make communities more resilient to flooding, rising seas and infrastructure vulnerabilities. The Maine Coastal Program's awards cover work in Boothbay, Gouldsboro, Addison and the Popham area of Phippsburg, with projects scheduled to begin this fall. The [Boothbay Register reported the awards](https://www.boothbayregister.com/article/maine-coastal-program-announces-299057-habitat-restoration-planning-grants/274931) Sept. 29, and the [Maine Office of Community Affairs describes the grant program](https://www.maine.gov/moca/funding/maine-coastal-program-habitat-restoration-planning-grant) as a one-time opportunity for planning, design and engineering.

The money is not a construction award. The program's official description says eligible activities include surveys, site characterization, inventories, preliminary and final designs, project prioritization and plan preparation, while subawards do not fund construction, land acquisition or site monitoring. That distinction matters for residents: the grants can produce the engineering and information needed for future work, but they do not by themselves mean a culvert will be replaced, a marsh will be rebuilt or a road will be redesigned.

In Boothbay, the town will conduct a town-wide assessment of road crossings. Consultants will evaluate each crossing for both coastal habitat-restoration potential and vulnerability to climate hazards, giving the town a way to rank future projects rather than treating crossings as isolated maintenance problems. The Maine Coastal Program says its broader work includes CoastWise tools for safe, cost-effective and climate-resilient tidal crossings, an issue that links transportation reliability with the health of wetlands and streams.

Gouldsboro's project will focus on the Sand Cove area and Grand Marsh. The plan calls for mapping sea-level-rise and storm-surge threats, basic infrastructure and natural resources, including the area's dune, freshwater and intertidal wetlands. Those layers are meant to help the town understand how future coastal transportation improvements could affect natural systems and where infrastructure decisions may increase or reduce vulnerability.

The Downeast Salmon Federation will work on a design supplement for a resilient crossing at Point Street on the West Branch Pleasant River in Addison. The project includes culvert-replacement design, geotechnical assessments and improvements to water infrastructure. Because the award supports design rather than construction, the immediate product will be a more developed basis for a later infrastructure decision at a crossing where road access and habitat conditions overlap.

The fourth project, led by the Kennebec Estuary Land Trust, will examine the vegetation and existing conditions of tidal marshes around Popham in Phippsburg. The trust plans to develop a restoration and resilience plan and evaluate the marshes' ability to absorb water as levels change. That work could help the community prepare for future flood events affecting the marsh and nearby infrastructure, although the announcement does not set a construction date or promise that a restoration project will follow.

The awards come through a one-time Habitat Restoration Planning opportunity funded under the federal Bipartisan Infrastructure Law through the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Office for Coastal Management. NOAA says the law supports grants and technical assistance for restoring coastal habitat and protecting ecological features that can reduce flooding and storm impacts. The federal context gives the Maine projects a larger purpose, but the local grants remain focused on planning and design.

Maine's Coastal Program is a federal, state and local partnership created under the Coastal Zone Management Act of 1972. The state says it coordinates assistance among public agencies, tribes, nonprofit groups and land trusts to manage coastal resources for public benefit. For the four awardees, the next step is to turn the grant-funded assessments and designs into usable plans. The work will give communities better information about where habitat restoration and infrastructure investments could provide the most resilience; whether those plans lead to funded construction will depend on later decisions and resources.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Maine awards $299,057 for coastal habitat planning
seoDescription: Four Maine communities and service providers will use $299,057 in grants for coastal habitat and resilience planning.
